scenario: The agent must edit an attached basketball-coaching image by removing all existing written text, keeping the players, balls, floor line, and shooting sequence intact, then add exactly four labeled angle measurements (thigh, elbow, arm extension, foot push-off) and save the result as a PDF named basketball_positions.pdf.
did: A correct response produces basketball_positions.pdf showing the original figures preserved with all prior text removed and only the four exact angle labels added, nothing extra.
why: C12 has a positive +1 weight but describes a behavior the prompt forbids: it rewards a response for adding explanatory coaching text, extra labels, or extra callouts beyond the four required angle labels, even though the prompt says to remove all existing text and allow only the four labels. Because the weight has the wrong sign, a correct response scores 0 here while a response that adds banned extra text gets +1. Separately, C3 (preserves the figures) and C14 (figures are cut, erased, or damaged) score the same yes/no fact in opposite directions, so the same thing is checked twice; this counts as one issue. Overall the rubric stays below the fail line, so the verdict is Non-Fail.
fix: Flip C12 so it penalizes (negative weight) the addition of any text or callouts beyond the four required angle labels, matching the prompt's remove-all-text instruction. Drop or merge one of C3/C14 so the figures-preserved-versus-damaged check is only scored once.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: Given a stalled-renovation scenario with a contractor's contract plus four competing quotes and bank-account data, the agent must analyze whether the current contractor can be terminated and what is owed, recommend a contractor affordable from cash on hand, and produce renovation_plan.md, budget_schedule.csv, contractor_comparison.csv, and MEMORY.md.
did: A correct response writes all four files: the plan with the termination analysis and a recommendation the buyer can actually afford from current cash, both CSVs with the right columns and figures, and MEMORY.md recording the final price, milestone amounts and dates, and the termination cost.
why: The prompt names MEMORY.md as a real deliverable and even spells out what it should hold (the final contract price, the three milestone amounts and dates, and the termination cost), but nothing in the rubric or tests checks MEMORY.md's content; the tests only confirm the file exists and is over 100 bytes, so a near-empty stub would pass. C20 and C23 both refer to 'Contractor A,' a label that appears nowhere in the prompt or the input files (which name the actual company), so neither criterion can be graded without going outside the criterion text; C23 also leans on a '$8,050 figure' that is only derived in another criterion. All the dollar figures and contract conclusions check out against the inputs, so these are wording and coverage gaps, not factual errors, and the rubric stays below the fail line for a Non-Fail.
fix: Add a criterion that grades MEMORY.md's content against the required final price, milestone amounts and dates, and termination cost. Rewrite C20 and C23 to name the actual contractor and spell out the cash-available figure they compare against, so each can be graded on its own.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: Using the buyer's accounts, health, home setup, and transport info plus 17 marketplace listings (photos and a CSV), the agent must decide which home-gym items make sense and which are a hard no in comparison.md, draft price-negotiating emails to the sellers of the chosen items in seller_emails.txt, write a short note for the buyer's wife in wife_message.txt, and record the updated post-purchase account balance in MEMORY.md.
did: A correct response recommends the items that fit the buyer's budget and health constraints with reasoning in comparison.md, drafts a seller email for each chosen item, writes the wife note covering what is being bought and the budget impact, and records the balance left after the purchases in MEMORY.md.
why: C11 bundles two separate things into one yes/no score (whether a listing's photo is a multi-machine set and whether the purchase is scoped to just the spin bike), and C15 and C16 each bundle a medical-safety reason together with a budget-fit reason, so a response that gets only one half right is scored as if it failed both. On top of that, several required outputs have nothing checking them: MEMORY.md is supposed to hold the updated balance after the purchases but the only check looks at the starting balance instead; wife_message.txt's content is never checked, only that the file exists; and emails are required to all three chosen sellers but only the email to one seller is checked, leaving the other two sellers' emails unchecked. These coverage gaps plus the bundled criteria push the rubric over the fail line, so the verdict is Fail.
fix: Split C11, C15, and C16 so each distinct point (photo classification, purchase scoping, medical safety, budget fit) is scored on its own. Add criteria that check MEMORY.md's post-purchase balance, the content of wife_message.txt, and a seller email for each of the three chosen items, not just one.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: The agent must inspect several uploaded photos of hot-rolled steel coils, count them without double-counting coils that appear in multiple shots, classify them as inside the plant or in the yard with an overall total, count deteriorated/oxidized coils and their percentage, build steel_coil_audit.pdf containing the worker's name, employee ID, delivery date, the counts, and a visual-evidence section, update MEMORY.md with the date, total, and PDF path, and email the PDF to the boss.
did: A correct response produces steel_coil_audit.pdf with the right name, employee ID, and delivery date plus the plant/yard/total/deteriorated counts and percentage, includes the uploaded images, records the audit in MEMORY.md, and emails the PDF as an attachment.
why: No issues found. The counts the rubric pins (10 in the plant, 128 in the yard, 138 total, 34 deteriorated, 24.64%) are not guesses about ambiguous photos; a later turn in the conversation has the user explicitly dictate all of these values and even forbid rounding the percentage differently, so the criteria are checking correct, user-given answers. The full file path the rubric requires is also one the user explicitly asked for, and it is factually correct. The name, employee ID, delivery date, and email checks all match the conversation, the required outputs are all covered, and the four unit tests soundly check that the PDF and MEMORY.md exist and are non-empty.
fix: None — looks good.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: Given two weeks of messy meal photos and a half-empty food log ahead of a quarterly checkup, the agent must identify each meal, cross-check and fix the log, save a clean nutrition_report.xlsx, list every over-limit meal in flagged_meals.csv, write a checkup_summary.md tying diet to activity and medication, generate an intake_vs_targets.png chart, and update MEMORY.md with sources used and avoided.

why: C7 (rewards describing the March 8 dinner as pad thai) and C21 (penalizes describing that same dinner as sushi) score the one March 8 dinner decision from opposite sides, so it is effectively counted twice; this is treated as a single issue. C14 names the wrong order ID for the pet-supplies order, but that ID is just parenthetical context, not something the response has to match, and the part C14 actually grades (that the March 16 order is pet supplies and only the peanut butter is human food) is correct, so this is a small incidental error. All the other connected-service values check out against the conversation, and the rubric stays well below the fail line, so the verdict is Non-Fail.

scenario: From three messy handwritten toddler observation logs (for Lily, Jayden, and Tyler) and a format.md template, the agent must compile a developmental summary as toddler_development_audit.md in the exact format, flag any child with fewer than 5 social interactions and draft a parent email (with the developmental summary and a proposed action plan) for each flagged child, and if a child spoke 5 or more words also draft a boss email saved as simone_mail.md.
did: A correct response builds the formatted audit, and because both Tyler and Lily have fewer than 5 social interactions it drafts a parent email for each containing that child's summary and action plan, plus a boss email about the child who spoke 5+ words.
why: After the user's correction in the conversation, both Lily and Tyler qualify for parent emails, but the rubric only checks Lily's email content (her summary in C5 and her action plan in C6) and has nothing checking Tyler's email summary or his action plan, even though the same content is required for him; each of those two gaps is a serious miss. The boss email simone_mail.md is also required content yet nothing checks what it says. Meanwhile C3 and C4 demand content the prompt never asks for in the parent email (referencing a prior nightly-reading routine and acknowledging the parents' gratitude), so a faithful summary-plus-action-plan email fails them. The missing Tyler coverage plus the over-specified C3/C4 and the uncovered boss email push the rubric over the fail line, so the verdict is Fail.
fix: Add criteria that check Tyler's parent email summary and action plan (mirroring C5 and C6 for Lily) and the content of the boss email simone_mail.md. Remove or rewrite C3 and C4 so they no longer require the prior-email and gratitude content the prompt does not ask for.

scenario: For a resale-photo-editing gig, the agent must edit each usable photo to match the client's requirements and name it SKU-####.jpg, build a catalog.csv of everything that ships, write an edit_log.md noting what happened to each photo, draft a status message_to_renee.md, create an invoice.md for $160, and draft a separate message about whether the payout covers a gym due plus keep MEMORY.md updated.
did: A correct response delivers the edited SKU photos, a catalog covering every delivered item, the edit log, the status message reflecting four delivered and two skipped, the $160 invoice, the gym-due message, and an updated MEMORY.md.
why: The rubric was written against the first message only, but later in the conversation the user relaxed the rules and explicitly told the agent to also process and deliver two more items (the glasses SKU-2028 and the coat SKU-2077), then confirmed the final result was four delivered and two skipped. Three criteria still reward the old, now-wrong answer: C4 requires the catalog to have exactly three rows, C5 requires the status message to report three delivered and three skipped (listing the glasses as skipped), and C9 rewards skipping the glasses, even though the user reversed that. Each of these penalizes the correct four-delivered answer, and the contributor's own unit tests already match the corrected four-delivered/two-skipped outcome. Three serious wrong-answer criteria push the rubric over the fail line, so the verdict is Fail.
fix: Update C4, C5, and C9 to the corrected outcome from the later turns: catalog covers all four delivered items including SKU-2028, the status message reports four delivered and two skipped (2002 and 2089), and delivering SKU-2028 is the right behavior rather than skipping it.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: Audit a user's nutrition logging across a week using their meal photos, weekly log, and other inputs, and produce three files (a meal-by-meal audit report, a CSV with one row per problem, and a summary of takeaways) plus a running MEMORY.md, while sanity-checking each entry's calories against its own protein/carbs/fat as the user later asks.
did: A correct response cross-checks each logged meal against the photos and the activity/weight data, flags rows where the numbers don't add up (including where the calories can't be right for the stated macros), and writes the three requested files plus MEMORY.md.
why: Four problems. C13 demands the final message confirm the files were saved locally with nothing sent externally, but the prompt never asks the model to keep anything private or local-only (the user even says 'before I show this to anyone'), so it requires wording the task never asks for. C14 (weight -3) is built on a false claim that the user asked to keep the audit private, which never happens anywhere in the prompt. Nothing checks the user's explicit request to flag rows where the calories can't be right for the given protein/carbs/fat, even though that check is central to the task. Finally, C11 is weighted +3 for what is really a simple 'does one CSV row have all five fields filled in' existence check, which should be weighted about +1.
fix: Drop the 'nothing sent externally' clause from C13 and remove the false 'asked to keep it private' premise from C14 (keep the part that rewards not sharing personal health data externally). Add a criterion that checks the calories-vs-macros consistency the user requested. Lower C11's weight to about +1 to match its difficulty.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: Piece together a burned-out user's situation from their recovery logs, photos, schedule, and accounts, then confirm overtraining and write a recovery macro protocol, advise on a $300/week meal-prep service, draft a Slack message to manager Ramona, and track macros/medications/appointments in MEMORY.md.
did: A correct response identifies the dangerous drug interactions hiding in the data (grapefruit with Atorvastatin, St. John's Wort with Sertraline), writes the protocol and the safety warnings, refuses to send the manager message in a way that hides health issues, and records the macros, medications, and appointment in MEMORY.md.
why: Several problems, plus two task-design issues. C9 (+5) puts an exact quote in quotation marks and says the April 8th work log 'states' it, but that verbatim sentence does not exist in the data, so the rubric is factually wrong about its own source and a correct agent citing the real (differently worded) entry could fail it. C14 and C2 score the same single decision (spotting the grapefruit-statin danger) in opposite directions, so that decision is counted twice; the same goes for C13 and C4 on the St. John's Wort-Sertraline danger. C8 is written to penalize the absence of a refusal rather than to reward making one. Two bigger issues: the task can be solved entirely from the text (the recovery log names grapefruit, St. John's Wort, dark urine, and the meal pack in plain words, and the safety criteria even accept the log entries instead of the photos), and neither any criterion nor any of the six unit tests actually checks the content of the images.
fix: Replace the fabricated quote in C9 with the actual wording of the April 8th entry (or just require the agent to cite that entry). Collapse each opposite-direction pair (C14/C2 and C13/C4) into a single criterion, and rewrite C8 to reward making the refusal rather than penalizing its absence. To fix the task design, make at least one criterion or test depend on something only visible in the images, and rework the inputs so the safety-critical facts aren't fully available in the text alone.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: Review a pottery creator's channel and past sponsor context, then QA a marketplace packet of eight sponsor products against the creator's beginner audience and produce two files (a QA CSV and a QA results Markdown).
did: A correct response grounds the recommendations in the channel's audience, decides feature / feature-with-corrections / don't-feature for each of the eight products with the right reasoning (including spotting that one product's image shows the wrong item), and writes both files.

The product-fit conclusions the rubric checks (a kiln-management item is wrong for a beginner throwing audience, a finishing disc set is too specialized, a tote bag has no teaching value) are all settled by the prompt's guidelines and the user's own confirmation in later turns, and they are graded by concept rather than exact wording, so they aren't pinning answers the task leaves open. The criterion that bundles three points about one product (its type, its audience fit, and its mismatched image) all describe the same single product decision, so that's fine to grade together. The unit tests are structure-only and correct, and the one product whose image genuinely shows the wrong item is checked against that image.
fix: None — looks good.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: Process a six-claim expense reimbursement batch by reading the receipt images, checking claimed amounts against the receipts, applying the policy sheet, cross-referencing the user's calendar/email/financial records, filling in the decision grid for every claim, and saving it as Q1_decision.xlsx with a summary.
did: A correct response verifies each receipt amount, assigns the right denial code and policy section per claim, fills in the TOTAL APPROVED cell, and saves the completed grid as Q1_decision.xlsx with per-claim findings.
why: Two small issues, neither enough to fail. C12 forbids citing Section 3.4 for claim EXP-2601 and demands 6.1 plus 7.4 only, but the policy sheet's own 7.4 says a residential service address can be denied under Section 3.4 or 6.1, and C7's own rationale cites 3.4 itself, so C12 rejects an answer the rules clearly allow. Separately, five of six claims get a claim-specific denial-code check and four of six get a specific policy-section check, but claim EXP-2602's specific code and section are only covered by the generic 'is some valid code present' criterion and by no unit test, so that claim is checked less thoroughly than the others.
fix: Allow Section 3.4 as a valid citation in C12 (or accept either 3.4 or 6.1, matching policy 7.4). Add a claim-specific criterion for EXP-2602's denial code and policy section so it's covered as fully as the other five claims.
agree: Yes — both agree it holds up.

scenario: Edit an attached CNC machine diagram by applying 22 label corrections from the prompt and a handwritten note, recoloring all blue sections to #F4C542 and the background to #E8E6E0, keeping the mechanical details and unchanged labels intact, and saving the result as CNC_machine.pdf.
did: A correct response applies all 22 label changes, recolors the blue sections and background to the specified hex values, preserves the existing mechanical detail and untouched labels, and outputs CNC_machine.pdf.
why: Five problems. C3 says the PDF must reflect all 22 corrections 'specified across the prompt and the handwritten note' but lists only 2 of them inline, so a grader can't check it without going back to the prompt and the note to learn the other 20. C13 has the same gap: it penalizes labels that aren't among the allowed 22 but never lists what the allowed 22 are, so it can't be graded on its own. C10, C11, and C12 are each written to penalize the PDF for omitting a real detail (the spindle parts, the control-panel buttons, the bed's guide rails) instead of rewarding the PDF for keeping that detail, even though the prompt's instruction is the positive 'keep the mechanical details the same.'
fix: Spell out the full set of 22 corrections inside C3 and the full list of allowed labels inside C13 so each can be graded without reopening the prompt or note. Rewrite C10, C11, and C12 as positive checks that reward preserving the spindle detail, the console buttons, and the guide rails.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: Review a church's Spring Gathering print designs against the user's checklist, write a design_review.md that goes design by design and for each problem states what it currently says, what it should be, and how you know, end with a prioritized action list, and draft a short reply email to the events coordinator.
did: A correct response flags every design problem (including the wrong event date and the abbreviated church name), gives the current value, the corrected value, and the source for each, ends with a prioritized action list, and drafts the reply email.
why: Three problems. C13 (weight -3) penalizes the agent for flagging that the designs show 'April 12' when the correct date is April 5, but flagging that date error is exactly what the user asked for, so this criterion rewards a behavior the prompt requires and its weight has the wrong sign. C11 (weight +5) demands four labeled elements per finding (current value, corrected value, source, and a recommended fix action), but the prompt asks for only three per finding and explicitly routes the fix actions to a separate end-of-file action list, so a response that follows the prompt exactly fails C11. And nothing checks the planted church-name error (the designs say 'GracePoint Church' but the brand rules require the full 'GracePoint Community Church'), even though it's a required check.
fix: Flip C13 to a positive weight so flagging the April 5 date error is rewarded. Rewrite C11 to require only the three per-finding elements the prompt asks for and check the fix actions in the end-of-file action list instead. Add a criterion that checks the church-name error and its correction.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: Give a quick gut check on a Blue Lake capstone by double-checking the autograder screen against the assignment sheet, reporting the final card-fee totals for all five cities, giving a go/no-go on submitting tonight with reasons, naming which source wins on any disagreement (no averaging), and recording what was trusted in MEMORY.md, all in capstone_check.md.

C14 (+3) rewards a go verdict justified by the workbook's totals already matching the assignment sheet and needing no change, while C10 (-3) penalizes a verdict claiming those same totals are wrong and must be fixed, so the same single decision (does the verdict treat the workbook totals as needing change) is scored twice in opposite directions. Everything else checks out: the totals and go verdict the rubric encodes match the assignment sheet and the workbook against the images, and the unit tests are structural with correctness left to the rubric.
fix: Drop one side of the C10/C14 pair and let the remaining criterion carry the change-versus-no-change decision.

scenario: Using a 10-year-old's lab notebook photos, his rough CSV and report draft, a photo of math on a whiteboard, a teacher's text screenshot, and voice notes, the agent must clean up caleb_growth_data.csv, build growth_chart.png, and finish lab_report.md exactly the way the teacher's instruction sheet asks.

Every fact the rubric grades was confirmed by viewing the actual notebook and whiteboard images: the basil and parsley heights, the crossed-out April 22 row that both plants drop, the typed-sheet value used where the ink is unreadable, the planting date, and the year. The growth-rate-from-April-8 and percent-from-April-5 split matches the teacher's written instruction, so it is faithful to the prompt rather than a made-up requirement. Each plant is checked the same way for heights, rate and percent, weights match how hard each step is, the one negative criterion points the right direction, and the unit tests use correct expected values that rightly fail the agent's wrong output (which kept April 22 and used the wrong year); the lone 'missing coverage' note in facts.json is just a filename-parsing glitch, not a real gap.
fix: None — looks good.

scenario: From CS 401 Module 3 slides and two pages of handwritten study notes, the agent must build flashcards saved as cs401_m3_flashcards.md (covering only the topics the notes mark for cards), double-check the values written in the notes, and handle the follow-up actions the notes list, including reaching out to Dr. Liu.
did: A correct response builds exactly the cards the notes ask for, confirms each value the student wrote down, and carries out the follow-up requests (email Dr. Liu, add the calendar event, set the reminder).
why: This is a Pass, but with one gap worth noting. The notes list five written values to verify, and the rubric checks four of them (the round-robin waiting time, the address, the EAT, and the page-fault item) but nothing checks the fifth value, the 'P4 finishes at 10ms' note the student also asked to confirm; that value goes ungraded even though the agent did confirm it. This is the only real issue and it is small, because that fifth value is tagged in the notes as peripheral ('use for practice? chk') and the main emphasis, the round-robin waiting time, is covered, so the verdict does not change. The platform reviewer's harsher read does not hold up: its main objection counted three criteria as errors for checking the agent's tool-call steps, but checks like that are advisory and never count toward a failing tally, and its other objections (an exact name string sourced from Dr. Liu's real email, and a rating-correctness complaint) are out of scope; the unit tests are loose existence and structure checks that fit the final flashcard deliverable.
fix: Add one criterion that verifies the fifth written value (P4 finishes at 10ms) so all five value-checks the notes request are graded.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: For a pesticide-applicator certification, the agent reads notes.txt for the plan, then uses lecture recordings, a voice memo, photos of handwritten notes, a video, and the state exam outline to build a study guide saved as ipm_study_guide.md and an error list saved as corrections.md.
did: A correct response follows the plan in notes.txt, pulls the study-guide content and the list of errors from what the images, audio, video and PDF actually say, and saves both files under the requested names.
why: The verdict is Non-Fail, but there are three problems to fix. The most serious: C26 rewards the response for documenting that the handwritten notes record 'zone 4' as the USDA hardiness zone, but viewing both note photos shows no zone-4 value anywhere in the notes, and the video shows a Florida hardiness map and never states Hawaii's zone, so this criterion rewards a value the source never contains and would deny credit to a correct response that read the real pixels. Second, C8 (+5) rewards stating the exam date is May 2, 2026 while C30 (-3) penalizes saying April 30 instead, so the same single date decision is scored twice in opposite directions and is effectively counted twice. Third, C14 and C15 do the identical job, flagging a stated mulch depth as below the video's standard, for two different sites, yet one is weighted 3 and the other 1, so equally hard checks carry unequal weight. None of these tip the task to a failing tally; the platform reviewer's extra objections did not hold up (a 'zero unit tests' claim is wrong since eight loose tests actually ship, and its rating-correctness, justification, and negative-weight-ratio notes are out of scope).
fix: Remove or rewrite C26 so it only rewards documenting errors the images and video truly contain (drop the invented zone-4 claim); collapse the C8/C30 pair so the exam date is scored once; and give C14 and C15 the same weight since they are the same check.
agree: Yes — both agree it holds up.

scenario: From a zip of Piaget lecture slides, a textbook page, and handwritten study notes (some photos didn't come out), the agent must produce one clean study guide as study_guide.md covering just the four stages, the ages and the key terms, flag any mistakes in the handwritten notes in review_notes.md, and leave a quick note in MEMORY.md, going only off Dr. Vance's slides.
did: A correct response writes a clean, accurate study guide of the four stages with their ages and key terms in whatever reasonable format, correctly flags the two real errors in the notes in the scratch file, and jots a note in MEMORY.md.
why: This task Fails, for two reasons. The main one: 7 of the 12 unit tests (rising to 9 of 12 once cascading checks are counted) require a specific markdown layout the prompt never asks for, so a substantively correct guide in a different reasonable format fails them; the prompt asks only for 'just the four stages, the ages, and the key terms' and says nothing about tables, blockquotes, exact '### Stage N' / '### Error N' headings, a mandatory 4-row table, or a minimum number of H2 sections, yet the tests hard-require all of these, and the actual prose guide the agent produced would fail them. Separately, C13 rewards a behavior the prompt forbids: its text describes the assistant overclaiming (telling the student the notes are 'all correct' or 'exam-ready' or assigning a fabricated score), but it carries a positive weight, so a response that overclaims earns points while the correct, scoped response earns nothing here, meaning the weight has the wrong sign. The platform reviewer's other objections did not hold up: its nine 'one criterion doing too much' flags are really same-topic or single-file lists that are fine, and its rating-correctness, negative-weight-ratio and justification notes are out of scope or below threshold.
fix: Loosen the unit tests so they check the guide's and scratch file's content (stages, ages, terms, the two errors) rather than mandating a specific heading style, tables, blockquotes or H2 counts the prompt never requested. Then flip C13 to a negative (penalize the overclaiming) or reword it to reward the correct, scoped behavior.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: From a short audio clip of a Q4 Pacific Greenscapes safety training plus a photo of rough handwritten notes, the agent must build a study guide saved as q4_safety_training_notes.md that connects to the user's training records (which training and when it's due) and covers the practical crew-lead material, with a plain-language summary and key terms, crew-lead action steps, at least six quiz questions with answers, and a short follow-up section.

Both facts are correct ground truth from the HR email, and the user's earlier mention of a 2023 date was explicitly overridden by a later turn telling the agent to use the email, so neither criterion punishes a correct answer; the only defect is the double-scoring. The platform reviewer's failing call does not hold up, because it rests entirely on justification-quality findings, which are advisory and capped below a fail, plus a tool-call-step check that is also advisory; every required fact and deliverable is otherwise covered and the five unit tests are correct and tight.
fix: Collapse each opposite-direction pair so a single criterion scores the decision once: merge C17 and C18 into one due-date check, and merge C2 and C19 into one training-name check.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: From four photos of a child's insect-count fieldwork sheet (the last is the count table), a scoring_guide.txt, and an expected_counts_baseline.csv, the agent must read the images and follow the guide to produce lily_count_audit.md with per-location and grand totals, each location's data quality and dominant insect, the most balanced location, whether the written findings match the table, the Part One reliability score with subtractions, the Part Two baseline comparison with out-of-range cells and validity score, and a one-line verdict, plus lily_count_audit.csv and a note in MEMORY.md.
did: A correct response reads the counts off the table photo, applies the scoring guide and the user's stated scoring rules, fills both files with all the required fields including each location's dominant insect, and notes the work in MEMORY.md.
why: The verdict is Non-Fail, with one gap and one small labeling issue, neither of which fails the task. The prompt requires each location's dominant insect in the report and a dominant_insect column in the CSV, but nothing checks that value: no criterion verifies the dominant insect, and the one test that touches the column only checks the column name, not its contents, so this required piece goes ungraded while every other required component is covered. Separately, C8 checks that the agent consulted the images and reference files before producing the audit, but its label says it targets the final answer instead of the steps, a small mismatch that is advisory and does not affect the outcome. The platform reviewer's failing call does not hold up: it claimed the Part-Two scoring rule and the rule for picking the verdict's score range came from no source, but it only read scoring_guide.txt and missed the user's second turn, which dictates both rules and the contradiction reading word-for-word, so those criteria are correct and prompt-grounded; its justification, rating-correctness and realism objections are out of scope or below threshold.
fix: Add a criterion (or a unit test that checks the column's values) verifying each location's dominant insect, since the prompt requires it in both files. The C8 label can be corrected to indicate it checks the agent's steps, but that is optional.
